name: Dhammasala Forest Monastery
tradition: Theravada Buddhism, Thai Forest Tradition (Dhammayut/Thammayut lineage)
technique: Anapanasati (breath meditation), walking meditation, and monastic Vinaya-based training
teacherAccess: Resident monks give Dhamma talks and meditation instruction, and lead a nightly 6pm Q&A session with retreatants
retreatOptions: Weekend to week-or-longer stays, May through September, length tailored to each applicant
schedule: Seasonal retreats May-September (weekends or weekdays by arrangement); weekly Saturday Dhamma class 5:30-6:30pm; daily lay food offering 10:30am-noon
cost: No fee charged — all retreats, talks, and materials are offered freely on a dana (donation) basis; monastery is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit

pricePerDay.notes: Pure dana model; no suggested or fixed retreat fee is published

foodNotes: Daily lay food offering around 11am, a mixture of Asian and Western dishes; not strictly vegetarian but vegetarian food is available; retreatants may take one, two, or three meals a day
workNotes: Guests are expected to assist with meal prep and kitchen cleanup and take part in an afternoon work period (~3pm) in the forest or gardens
about: Dhammasala Forest Monastery is a Theravada Buddhist monastery in the Thai Forest (Dhammayut) tradition, founded in 2000 by Ajahn Khemasanto on a wooded property in Perry, Michigan. The monastery offers seasonal retreats from May through September, ranging from a weekend to a week or longer, set in a secluded forest with meditation huts, tent platforms, a gazebo, and a meditation hall. Retreatants observe the Eight Precepts, keep "wise silence," and follow the monastery's daily rhythm of alms-style food offerings, quiet practice periods, and an afternoon work period, with resident monks available for meditation instruction and a nightly Dhamma Q&A. All teachings, retreats, and printed materials are offered freely on a dana (donation) basis. The community includes founder Ajahn Khemasanto along with resident monks Tan Thittisampanno and Tan Mahaviro.
